newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korea takes its time on defector debriefing.
newsitem.headline: South Korea takes its time on defector debriefing.

text.p: After landing the most important catch of the Cold War in Korea -- Pyongyang defector Hwang Jang-yop -- South Korea's spy agency on Monday made clear it did not intend to rush into a debriefing.

Officials in South Korea and its allies, particularly the United States, are agog at the prospect of Hwang, North Korea's top ideologue, spilling the innermost secrets of the Stalinist state as it slides into famine and economic ruin.

U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen, in a television interview on Sunday, said South Korea had agreed to let the United States interrogate Hwang "to find out what is in the hearts and minds of the Korean leadership".
But Hwang's handlers at Seoul's Agency for National Security Planning were taking their time.
"We will not hasten our investigation. Mr Hwang Jang-yop needs time to regain his psychological stability," one security official said.
First priority on Monday was a medical checkup for Hwang, 74, who appeared tense and emotional after arriving on Sunday from the Philippines with an aide.
Hwang hid for a month in the Philippines after being spirited out of Beijing where he had sought asylum at South Korea's consular office on February 12.

If he talks freely -- and bodyguards can protect his life -- the chief architect of North Korea's guiding ideology of "juche", or self-reliance, will offer an unprecedented window into perhaps the most reclusive nation on earth.
The Chosun Ilbo daily said Hwang was expected to unveil a treasure trove of intelligence that could lead to a "big bang" in inter-Korean relations.
"There's no doubt Hwang will help us understand the current state of affairs more accurately," Deputy National Unification Minister Lee Ho told Reuters.

Asked if Hwang's insights could prompt South Korea to rewrite its North Korea policy, Lee said: "It is premature to talk about policy changes. We have to carefully listen to what he says and sift through his remarks".
After arriving on Sunday, Hwang warned that North Korea had rejected the path of reform and dialogue with the South and was bent on war.
His ominous message came as Seoul and Washington tried to convince Pyongyang to join landmark talks aimed at securing a lasting peace to replace an armistice that ended the 1950-53 Korean War.
A foreign ministry official said he did not expect Hwang would influence North Korea's response to a U.S.-South Korean proposal for four-nation peace talks, also including China.
"His defection took place in February and I don't see why the issue will affect the talks in New York now," he said.

Officials from North and South Korea and the United States met in New York on Sunday but made no progress over Pyongyang's participation in the peace talks, foreign ministry spokesman Lee Kyu-hyung said.
"Although North Korea called the unscheduled meeting, it showed no change in its earlier position," Lee said.
Pyongyang delegates twice failed to show up last week for senior-level meetings arranged to hear North Korea's reply to the proposal for four-nation peace talks.
Another such meeting has been rescheduled for Monday.

On Wednesday, Pyongyang essentially accepted the peace talks proposal but then tied acceptance to demands for additional food aid, Lee said. Seoul and Washington say substantial aid can be discussed only after Pyongyang sits at the peace table.
